report:
## Conclusion

**No—not as routine treatment for knee osteoarthritis.** Arthroscopy (lavage/washout, “clean-up”/debridement, or removal of degenerative meniscal tissue) does not provide a clinically meaningful, lasting improvement in pain or function compared with non-surgical care or placebo surgery for most people with knee OA.

**Why the evidence is persuasive:**
- A randomized trial in people with moderate-to-severe knee OA compared arthroscopic surgery plus optimized physical/medical treatment with optimized treatment alone; the trial found no added benefit from surgery.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18784099/
- A systematic review/meta-analysis assessing arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease (including OA and degenerative meniscal tears) evaluated both benefits and harms; its overall evidence base does not support the procedure for middle-aged or older people with degenerative knee pain.  
  https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/49/19/1229
- The Cochrane review specifically evaluates arthroscopic surgery—including debridement and partial meniscectomy—against placebo or non-surgical treatment in degenerative knee disease.  
  https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease
- Accordingly, the AAOS guideline states that arthroscopic lavage and/or debridement is **not recommended** when the primary diagnosis is knee OA (moderate-strength recommendation).  
  https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf

This does **not** mean arthroscopy is never appropriate: an orthopaedic assessment may be warranted for a different, discrete problem—such as a truly locked knee from an acute displaced tear or loose body. But that is distinct from treating osteoarthritis itself.
